Prevention: COCOBOD authorised seed gardens (commonly called mixed hybrids)
Remove chupons (green basal/side growths) as these are succulent and attractive both as feeding and egg-laying sites
Remove alternative host plants such as young silk cotton trees and kola (Cola spp.)

Monitoring: Mirids are found throughout the year especially duning
They cause damage to seedling, cherelles and shoots by sucking the sap from their tissues
Feeding puncture marks appear as water- soaked patches that turn black after 2-3 days.
On young pods these are usually black round lesions near the stalk facing the trunk and the pods wilt.
Feeding on shoots and stems can cause splits (cankers) and die back.
Inspect cocoa plants up to hand height monthly for the presence of mirids and feeding lesions on pods and shoots
Monthly examinations of whole plants for lesions on fan branches and die back (browning of leaves on branches from the tip down)
Monthly inspection of broken cocoa canopies for mirids and lesions on fresh chupons
Damage on mature pods over three months old is not important but spray when average numbers reach 6 mirids per 10 trees
Direct Control: Maintain continuous but well pruned canopy as broken canopy allows sunlight to reach the forest floor and promotes fresh chupon (new shoots) growth which attracts mirids.
If the canopy is broken replace dead trees or plant plantain as it grows quickly and closes the canopy
The pesticides listed below can be used to manage mirids on cocoa.

Restrictions: Wear protective clothing, hat, overall, gloves, goggles, nose mask, boots
Do not eat, drink or smoke during application
Do not spray near streams or rivers or wash spray equipment in running/drinking water
Apply using a motorised mistblower on monthly basis beginning from
November (to avoid contamination of beans at peak harvest).
Spraying can be carried out in
Jan-July when mirid numbers and damage is high - 2 applications at monthly intervals.
For infested areas/ pockets spot spraying can be carried out.
